item.title: JACS: Facile Aryl Radical Generation via ART Process Enables Diverse 1,2-Aryl Heteroatom Functionalization of Alkenes
item.description:
Hongyu Wang, Ruonan Du, Wenxuan Ma, Yang Li, Junkai Fu
The emerging amino radical transfer (ART) offers an indirect route for converting readily accessible boronic acids and their derivatives into the corresponding radical species, thereby circumventing the high oxidation potential and limited substrate scope inherent to conventional direct oxidation methods. Despite considerable advances in alkyl radical generation, extending this strategy to the formation of high-energy aryl radicals has remained elusive. Herein, using N-chlorodialkylamines as a specific aminyl radical source, we demonstrate the successful generation of aryl radicals via ART. This robust platform enables the three-component 1,2-aryl heteroatom functionalization of alkenes through a radical-polar crossover pathway and exhibits broad compatibility with challenging basic dialkylamines, as well as arylamines, alcohols, and carboxylic acids. Mechanistic studies reveal that the low reduction potential of N-chlorodialkylamines enables efficient single-electron transfer to produce aminyl radicals, which trigger the subsequent ART process to generate aryl radicals under mild conditions. This pathway effectively suppresses competing two-component amination while preventing rapid aryl radical decomposition.

item.title: ACS Nano: Molecular-Reinforced Framework of FAPbI3 Quantum Dots for High-Performance Near-Infrared Light-Emitting Diodes
item.description:
Po Lu, Qi Liu, Rui Li, Danpeng Gao, Zhe Wang, Wenli Xin, Shuxuan Liao, Xiao Wu, et al.
FAPbI3 perovskite quantum dots (PQDs) exhibit great promise for next-generation optoelectronic devices owing to their excellent near-infrared (NIR) emission properties and low-cost solution processability. However, their soft lattice, characterized by dynamic [PbI6]4– octahedral vibrations, presents a fundamental barrier to efficient and stable NIR light-emitting diodes (LEDs). Here, we report a molecular lattice reinforcement strategy using 4-(trifluoromethyl)benzamidine hydrochloride (TFBH) as an in situ multifunctional surface modifier. Strong multisite interactions between TFBH and the PQD surface restrict dynamic fluctuations of the [PbI6]4– framework, while simultaneously passivating surface defects and suppressing ion migration. The synergistic effects of lattice reinforcement and surface passivation enable near-unity photoluminescence quantum yield, enhanced exciton binding energy, and improved electrical conductivity. Consequently, the rigid NIR PQD LEDs achieve a high external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 24.8% at 758 nm, along with a nearly 18-fold enhancement in operational lifetime. To further demonstrate the versatility of this strategy, we extend our approach to flexible devices, which achieve an EQE of 20.9%, the highest efficiency reported for flexible NIR perovskite LEDs.

item.title: Nano Letters: Coordination-Mediated Decoupling-Reconstruction Enables Semisolid Phase Regeneration of Spent Cathodes
item.description:
Pengrong Zhang, Yan Wang, Tingzhou Yang, Yunjie Cui, Xia Sun, Xiaoyi Zhang, Haodi Dong, Chunyong Liang, et al.
Achieving sustainable recycling of lithium (Li)-ion batteries requires a paradigm shift from conventional elemental recovery toward chemistry-guided regeneration of functional electrode materials. Here, we establish a coordination-mediated semisolid regeneration paradigm that directly reconstructs spent LiFePO4 into high-performance LiMn0.6Fe0.4PO4. Within an oxalate-coordinated reaction field, proton-assisted lattice deconstruction is coupled with selective elemental decoupling, extracting Li while retaining Fe as a structurally defined ferrous oxalate intermediate. The recovered Li is converted into LiH2PO4, while the oxalate intermediate serves as a regulated precursor for olivine reconstruction. Subsequent thermal transformation promotes homogeneous cation redistribution, conformal carbon coating, and crystallographic re-equilibration, yielding a structurally ordered and electronically homogeneous cathode. The regenerated material delivers 156.5 mAh g–1 at 0.2 C and retains 91.2% of its initial capacity after 1000 cycles at 2 C. This work establishes semisolid regeneration as a chemistry-guided route for value-added upcycling of spent polyanionic cathodes.

item.title: Nano Letters: Modulating Lipid Nanoparticles for Spleen Targeted RNA Delivery
item.description:
Kseniia Vlasova, Noorjahan Aibani, Mrinmoy Sanyal, Marco Herrera, Avisek Deyati, Pierrot Harvie, Seba Jumaa, Daniel Arriaza, et al.
Conventional lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) efficiently deliver RNA to the liver in preclinical models, but achieving clinically relevant delivery to other tissues remains a major challenge. Here we vary ionizable lipids and stabilizers along with optimizing formulation parameters for passive targeted delivery of circular RNA without permanently charged lipids. We generated a library of 216 LNP formulations and screened them in vitro in Jurkat cells and human primary T-cells. The lead candidates were explored for their efficacy in vivo via multiple routes of administration. Our results show that optimization of the lipid ratio decreases hepatic delivery while enhancing splenic accumulation. This improved tissue tropism to the spleen induces distinct transcriptomic remodeling in vivo compared with conventional SM-102 LNPs. These findings demonstrate that extrahepatic targeting of LNPs can be achieved without altering charge of the LNPs and further reveal that hepatic detargeting efficiency could be influenced by the immune status of the recipient.

item.title: ACS Nano: Physics-Structured Literature Learning Enables Transferable Ranking and Domain-Aware Prioritization of Carbon Nanotube Growth Conditions
item.description:
Yanlong Zhao, Fei Wang, Aike Xi, Qixuan Cai, Khaixien Leu, Kangkang Wang, Rufan Zhang
Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) enables scalable carbon nanotube (CNT) growth, but synthesis knowledge remains fragmented across catalyst chemistries, growth modes, process conditions, and incompletely reported outcomes, limiting the transfer between studies. Here, we reconstruct 3,496 synthesis records spanning nearly three decades and map each experiment onto a shared physical representation of catalyst and nucleation state, carbon supply, transport, and process boundaries across five CVD growth modes. Cross-paper and chronological validation revealed strongly target-dependent transfer: diameter retained the clearest ranking, with Spearman correlation of 0.737 under paper-grouped cross-validation and 0.609 under chronological holdout, whereas growth quality, IG/ID, orientation, and a multiproperty composite outcome showed weaker or less stable ordering. The physics-structured representation preserved useful ranking information while revealing target-specific reliance on physical descriptors and enabling the consistent reconstruction of candidate states. Conditional quantile predictions and historical replay further showed cutoff-dependent values for prioritizing favorable CNT growth conditions subsequently reported in the literature. Combining these rankings with literature-domain support and foldwise ranking stability yields traceable priorities for experimental evaluation rather than universal or experimentally validated CNT growth recipes.

item.title: JACS: Oxygen-Stabilized Barium Manganese Nitride Framework Enables Low-Temperature Ammonia Decomposition
item.description:
Qing Guo, Shiyao Wang, Jiang Li, Hideo Hosono, Masaaki Kitano
Rational design of stable active sites from earth-abundant elements is essential for replacing precious metals and advancing low-temperature ammonia decomposition for hydrogen delivery. Early 3d transition metals are attractive because of their abundance and low cost, yet their strong nitrogen binding often hinders catalytic turnover. Here, we report a novel oxynitride, Ba6Mn2N6O, in which lattice oxygen coordinates with Ba to stabilize an active barium manganese nitride framework comprising isolated [MnN3]δ− units and electron-confined Ba6 cavities. These Ba6 cavities promote NH3 adsorption and activation, lattice nitrogen enables N–N coupling, and redox-active Mn centers mediate electron transfer from N to H. This cooperative mechanism enables MgO-supported Ba6Mn2N6O to outperform leading nonprecious-metal catalysts and many Ru-based catalysts at 450 °C, while reducing transition-metal costs by 2–4 orders of magnitude relative to Co and Ru. This work demonstrates the potential of rationally engineered, earth-abundant active sites to migrate the reliance on Ru and advance ammonia as a global-scale hydrogen carrier.

item.title: ACS Nano: Restoration of Rb Tumor Suppressor Function in Retinoblastoma with Intravitreal GPC2-Targeted RB1 mRNA Lipid Nanoparticles
item.description:
Grant P. Grothusen, Hooda Said, Kendra S. McDaid, Evan Cresswell-Clay, Jaden L. Franks, Stephanie Matlaga, Rakan El-Mayta, Kristopher R. Bosse, et al.
Loss of RB1, the first identified tumor suppressor gene, is an oncogenic hallmark of retinoblastoma, a malignant pediatric tumor of the developing retina. Restoration of RB1 and consequent reactivation of the Rb tumor suppressor protein represent an ideal gene therapy against the disease. Here, we employed lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) targeting GPC2, a retinoblastoma-specific cell surface antigen, to deliver codon-optimized, synthetic RB1 messenger (m)RNA into retinoblastoma cells. LNPs conjugated to an antibody against GPC2 using strain-promoted azide–alkyne cycloaddition chemistry demonstrated enhanced uptake and expression longevity of mRNA in retinoblastoma cells in vitro and in an intraocular retinoblastoma murine model after intravitreal administration. Mechanistically, Rb tumor suppressor restoration via GPC2-targeted RB1 mRNA-LNPs (aGPC2/LNP-RB1) resulted in decreased retinoblastoma viability in vitro concomitant with global transcriptomic remodeling toward neuronal differentiation after repeated treatments. Critically, clinically achievable doses of intravitreal aGPC2/LNP-RB1 inhibited the growth of intraocular retinoblastoma xenografts in vivo and displayed acute but transient and manageable intraocular inflammation without systemic toxicities in immunocompetent hosts. Collectively, our findings support further development toward clinical translation of aGPC2/LNP-RB1 mRNA therapy for children with refractory intraocular retinoblastoma.

item.title: Nano Letters: Temperature-Dependent Relaxation Pathways in Perovskite BIC Exciton-Polariton Condensation
item.description:
Yuexing Xia, Xin Zeng, Tongcai Yuan, Yiyang Gong, Xiaotian Bao, Shuai Yue, Jianhui Fu, Wenna Du, et al.
Exciton-polariton systems supported by bound states in the continuum (BICs) constitute an appealing platform for integrated on-chip quantum photonic devices, benefiting from their ultrahigh quality factors, enhanced light–matter coupling, and long-range spatial coherence. However, the lasing behaviors of BIC lasers under variable-temperature environments, particularly the microscopic relaxation pathways governing polariton condensate formation, remain ambiguous. Here we report a systematic investigation of temperature-driven condensation dynamics in perovskite BIC exciton-polaritons over 4–300 K, using steady-state and ultrafast spectroscopic characterizations. We identify three distinct temperature regimes governing polariton population relaxation: phonon-assisted scattering prevails above 226 K; a phonon bottleneck governs between 105 and 226 K originating from inhibited phonon-mediated relaxation; and exciton-reservoir-assisted population transfer dominates below 105 K, accompanied by anomalous line-width broadening of the polariton condensate. These results uncover the temperature-modulated relaxation physics of perovskite BIC exciton-polaritons and provide practical guidelines for optimizing polariton lasers and integrated quantum photonic hardware.

item.title: JACS: Chemoselective On-Resin Synthesis of Imide and Thiosuccinimide Functionalized Peptides: Enabling Tunable Retro-Thia-Michael Bioconjugations
item.description:
Andrew Siow, Yu-Ting Hsiao, Jinwei Sun, Yuliana Yosaatmadja, Lara D. Browne, Johanes K. Kasim, Haoyun Li, Yu Wang, et al.
We report a site-selective synthetic methodology for accessing 5- and 6-membered imide and thiosuccinimide functional groups on-resin via Fmoc solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS). The formation of these heterocyclic frameworks is enabled by a modified Corey–Nicolaou activation strategy, which is kinetically favored via a 5/6-exo-trig cyclization according to Baldwin’s rules. The incorporation of the versatile 2-pyridyl thiosuccinimide moiety, acting as a masked maleimide, facilitates chemoselective aqueous solution-phase bioconjugations via a retro-thia-Michael pathway. This platform accommodates a broad scope of peptide modifications, including intramolecular cyclization, peptide stapling, small-molecule/peptide conjugation, and biocompatible protein conjugation. Furthermore, the resulting thiosuccinimide constructs can undergo controlled hydrolysis to yield stable acyclic thioether-linked conjugates, providing uniform peptide derivatives that are highly resistant to subsequent retro-thia-Michael degradation.

item.title: JACS: From Localized Mn Defect to Oxygen Loss: The Interplay of Jahn–Teller and Pseudo–Jahn–Teller Distortions
item.description:
Tong Wang, Yuhang Zhuang, Zhang Wen, Xiaohui Zhu, Shuang Li, Ping He, Qi Fan, Fan Kong, et al.
Developing structurally robust layered manganese-based cathodes is pivotal for sodium-ion batteries, yet inhibiting their lattice collapse remains an ongoing challenge. Here, we unravel a previously overlooked degradation mechanism in Na-birnessite, revealing that the localized Pseudo–Jahn–Teller (PJT) distortion exerts a much more catastrophic and dominant impact on framework failure than the traditionally emphasized cooperative Jahn–Teller (JT) effect. We show that during desodiation, the coexistence of structural Mn vacancies and crystal water triggers a strong Mn4+-related PJT distortion, accelerating irreversible oxygen loss at unexpectedly low voltages. To circumvent this vulnerability, we synthesize a Mn-vacancy-suppressed Na0.62Cu0.1Mn0.9O2·0.35H2O cathode. The substantial reduction of Mn vacancies breaks the critical electronic-vibrational coupling pathways, successfully mitigating the localized PJT modes and securing excellent cyclability (80% retention over 1000 cycles). When coupled with a hard carbon anode, the practical viability of this design is fully demonstrated. This discovery shifts the research focus from macro-JT suppression to local-PJT mitigation, establishing an essential guideline for designing degradation-resistant intercalation electrodes.

item.title: Nano Letters: Self-Assembling Peptide Materials for the Treatment of Infectious and Biofilm-Related Diseases
item.description:
Christian S. Carnero Canales, Miguel D’Agostino dos Santos, Subham Kumar Vishwakarma, Cesar Augusto Roque-Borda, Rafael Miguel Sábio, Fernando Rogério Pavan, Hélder A. Santos
Antimicrobial peptides frequently lose efficacy in biofilms because heterogeneous extracellular matrixes restrict access to microbial cells and compromise peptide stability. Self-assembly can modify these constraints by controlling the physical state in which the peptides encounter pathogens. This review examines how molecular interactions and infection-associated signals govern supramolecular transitions and how these changes influence antimicrobial activity. A recurring challenge is balancing penetration into biofilms with sufficient retention and contact at microbial interfaces: structures that persist locally may struggle to reach deeply embedded cells, whereas more mobile assemblies may provide limited exposure. Yet, many reported improvements remain difficult to attribute specifically to self-assembly because peptide chemistry and formulation effects are not adequately controlled. Establishing clear relationships between the assembly state and biological function will require comparisons under infection-relevant conditions and should inform the design of peptide materials for persistent infections.

item.title: ACS Nano: Wireless Magnetoelectric Patch Promotes Infected Wound Scarless Healing by Macrophage Metaboimmune Reprogramming
item.description:
Wanli Song, Shuo Liu, Ziqi Liu, Boon Chin Heng, Genmao Zhang, Jinchu Liang, Zhen Liu, Yaojin Wang, et al.
Infected cutaneous wounds often lead to fibrotic scarring. Current treatment modalities often fail to dynamically regulate the sequential repair cascade, especially infection control, immune regulation, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Herein, this study develops a remotely controllable therapeutic strategy via a wireless magnetoelectric system. Specifically, a magnetoelectric patch is designed and developed by incorporating magnetoelectric CoFe2O4@BiFeO3 core–shell nanoparticles (CFO@BFO NPs) and a conductive reduced graphene oxide (rGO) network into a hydrogel matrix. Under an external alternating magnetic field, the magnetoelectric patch initially suppresses bacterial survival by inducing oxidative stress, disrupting membrane transporters, and impairing metabolic homeostasis. Subsequently, magnetoelectric stimulation induces the reprogramming of inflammatory macrophages from glycolysis-dominant metabolism to mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) via the PI3K-AKT pathway. Interestingly, this immunometabolic transition is accompanied by the activation of lipid metabolism and efferocytosis pathways for extracellular matrix remodeling. The scarless healing therapeutic effect was validated in mouse full-thickness and rabbit ear wound models. Notably, the magnetoelectric patch outperformed a commercial growth factor dressing in preclinical minipigs, achieving a higher wound healing rate and a reduction in scar-related parameters. Collectively, these findings demonstrate wireless magnetoelectric stimulation as a dynamically controllable therapeutic strategy for coordinating antibacterial and immunometabolic therapies to promote scarless wound healing.

item.title: Nano Letters: Au-Free Hexagonal SiGe Nanowires and Quantum Dots
item.description:
Denny Lamon, Marijn J. J. M. V. Hendrikx, Marvin M. Jansen-Zilles, Ries Koolen, Marcel A. Verheijen, Erik P. A. M. Bakkers
Ge and SiGe alloys are promising materials for next-generation optoelectronics. In their hexagonal crystal phase, they exhibit a direct bandgap, unlike their cubic counterparts, enabling efficient infrared light emission with a wavelength tunable through the Ge content. Quantum confinement has also been demonstrated in quantum wells, quantum wires, and quantum dots (QDs). However, quantum wires and QDs are typically realized in Au-catalyzed nanowires, despite the fact that Au is incompatible with CMOS technology and introduces nonradiative recombination centers that can reduce emission efficiency. In this work, we demonstrate the growth of high-quality hexagonal SiGe nanowires and QDs using Ga as a catalyst. Nanowire length and diameter were precisely controlled, while QDs with Ge concentrations up to 80% were achieved within the predicted direct-bandgap regime. This Au-free approach provides a viable route toward CMOS-compatible hexagonal SiGe nanostructures with potentially enhanced light-emission efficiency, bringing integrated group-IV light sources closer to practical realization.

item.title: JACS: Regioswitchable and Enantioselective Dialkylation of Alkenes: Modular Access to Chiral β- and γ-Amino Esters
item.description:
Xiao Li, Wenfeng Liu, Yiqun Zhang, Xin Wei, Wangqing Kong
Catalytic alkene difunctionalization is a powerful strategy for the rapid assembly of complex molecular architectures and has wide applications in synthetic chemistry. However, selective construction of two distinct alkyl–alkyl bonds across the C═C bond in alkenes remains a formidable challenge. Existing methods heavily rely on directing group strategy or specific ground-state radical traps, and the regio- and enantioselective dialkylation of alkenes remains elusive. Furthermore, a method enabling the simultaneous access to two regioisomers in an enantioselective manner has not yet been devised. Herein, we present a regioswitchable and enantioselective alkene dialkylation via photoredox/nickel dual catalysis. This approach provides a unique technique for the modular and practical synthesis of optically pure natural and unnatural β- and γ-amino esters, cornerstones of chemistry and biology. This method utilizes readily available and abundant unactivated alkyl halides and protic C(sp3)–H bonds as coupling partners, demonstrating broad substrate applicability as well as excellent regio- and enantioselectivity. The key to the success lies in the ingenious utilization of the rate difference in the generation of alkyl radicals between alkyl iodides and alkyl bromides via halogen-atom transfer. Furthermore, the synthetic practicality of this regiodivergent protocol has been demonstrated in the enantioselective synthesis of pharmaceutically relevant molecules.

item.title: JACS: Nucleotide-Resolved Conformational Analysis of Nascent RNA Chains within the Bacterial Transcription Elongation Complex by MAS-DNP Solid-State NMR
item.description:
Jyothirmayi Unnikrishnan Geethadevi, Johanna Becker-Baldus, Anna Wacker, Julia Wirmer-Bartoschek, Boris Fürtig, Sanjay Dey, Albert Weixlbaumer, Clemens Glaubitz, et al.
In all kingdoms of life, multisubunit RNA polymerases transcribe DNA to RNA. Both genomic DNA and newly transcribed RNA play key roles in transcription initiation, elongation, and termination. For example, a stretch of uridine residues at the 3′-end of the nascent RNA chain serves as a trigger to terminate transcription, release the nascent RNA chain, and disassemble bacterial transcription elongation complexes (ECs). It has remained unclear how the transcript can trigger termination if polyuridine stretches are synthesized. Here, we establish an approach that combines site-selective 13C/15N labeling of uridines with magic-angle-spinning dynamic nuclear polarization (MAS-DNP) NMR to probe the nascent transcript residue by residue within a reconstituted, stalled Escherichia coli transcription EC. We read out the 3′-terminal U-tract in the free RNA and in complexes stalled at two registers to investigate conformational heterogeneity in the rU–dA hybrid duplex. Our results suggest that the internal uridines adopt a stable A-form (C3′-endo) conformation in the hybrid duplex. This conformation remains unchanged within the EC, whereas the 3′-terminal residue is selectively perturbed within the complex. Solid-state NMR data collected on tailored isotopically labeled ECs resolve single-residue differences in conformation inside an assembled transcription EC, opening a route to study the nascent RNA at sites relevant to pausing and termination by MAS-DNP.

item.title: JACS: Antibody-Guided Photocatalytic Cross-Linking Enables Targeted Protein Structure Elucidation
item.description:
Sebastian N. Steiner, Clinton Yu, Marco Baumann, Arend Keller, Simon D. Widmer, Sandra Goetze, André Zwicky, Alexander Leitner, et al.
The structure and dynamics of proteins underlie virtually all biological processes, and there is a growing need for methods that can interrogate protein conformations in complex mixtures. Chemical cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) addresses this need. Still, it relies on untargeted, diffusible cross-linkers that react with any accessible residue, limiting both selectivity and effective use of cross-linking capacity. Here, we report an antibody-guided, photocatalytic cross-linking platform that enables targeted structural elucidation of proteins of interest within complex samples. We developed HyProX, a trifunctional histidine-specific cross-linker that combines two hydrazide groups to trap light-induced histidine intermediates and a phosphonic acid handle for enrichment. Building on LUX-MS photocatalytic proximity labeling, singlet oxygen generators (SOGs) conjugated to antibodies locally convert histidines on the target protein into short-lived endoperoxide intermediates, which HyProX selectively captures to form His–His cross-links in a strictly light-dependent manner. Using model peptides, we demonstrate efficient formation of cross-linked products and show that HyProX forms a C–N bond that undergoes preferential collision-induced dissociation (CID), releasing signature fragment pairs that MS3 can directly sequence. Applying antibody-guided HyProX cross-linking to human transferrin in a multiprotein mixture and human serum yields an increase in cross-linked spectral matches and higher unique cross-link coverage for the target protein compared to untargeted conditions, with all observed cross-links mapping on the known crystal structure. Together, these results establish antibody-guided, photocatalytic His–His cross-linking with HyProX as a conceptually new XL-MS platform that provides spatiotemporal control, residue selectivity, and an intrinsic MS-based decross-linking readout for targeted protein structure analysis in complex biological mixtures.

item.title: JACS: Rh2C3− Cluster-Driven Nitrogen Activation: Trapping a High-Energy Intermediate
item.description:
Shi-Hu Du, Zi-Heng Zhang, Shi-Jun Wang, Gang Li, Xiang-Tao Kong, Wen-Wu Xu, Shi-Bo Cheng, Ling Jiang, et al.
Converting inert and globally abundant molecules such as N2 into useful chemicals is central to sustainable energy and environmental chemistry. Herein, we investigate the gas-phase reaction of the Rh2C3− anion with N2 using mass spectrometry, anion photoelectron spectroscopy, and quantum chemical calculations. The experimental spectra of Rh2C3− and Rh2C3N2− exhibit closely similar features, indicating a preserved electronic core upon N2 attachment. Theoretical analysis further reveals that the end-on N2 adsorption complex is a trapped high-energy intermediate whose subsequent transformation is prevented by an activation barrier that necessitates additional energy input, and that this complex exhibits superior performance in the coconversion of diverse energy-bearing gas molecules. Furthermore, the subsequent application of oriented external electric fields provides a nondestructive and continuously adjustable means of modifying the intrinsic barrier heights, thereby effectively switching the reaction mechanism. These findings elucidate the complex reaction network of Rh2C3− with N2, establish a reliable spectroscopic fingerprint for identifying isomeric intermediates, and provide fundamental insights into electronic control strategies for catalytic nitrogen activation.

item.title: JACS: Departing Pathways in Aza-Diarylethene Photoswitching: Elucidating the Role of the Central Ring Allows Reprogramming of the Photoresponse
item.description:
Marc Villabona, Martina Hartinger, Katharina Fuchs, Maximilian Sacherer, Carolin Müller, Henry Dube
Aza-diarylethenes (aza-DAEs) are an emerging class of molecular photoswitches that allow reversible C–N bond formation and cleavage upon irradiation. They not only show high potential as T-type photochromes but also offer exciting opportunities for the exploration of unique reactivity control. Two types of these photoswitches are currently being investigated, which differ substantially in the nature of their metastable states. While classical DAE behavior is found in perfluorinated thiazole derivatives, an unexpected zwitterion formation and concomitant aromatization is observed for nonfluorinated pyrimidine derivatives. The latter offers reversible control over intramolecular charge separation and intrinsic three-state photoswitching. Their metastable state unleashes thiolate reactivity, which can be harnessed, e.g., in photoinitiation applications for smart polymer generation. Despite this promising progress, the reason for the divergent photochemical behavior in aza-DAEs is not yet understood. Here, we show that substitution of the central five-membered ring is responsible for the different photochemical outcomes and nature of the metastable state. Furthermore, our computational results provide systematic insights into the structural factors governing the relative stability of the neutral closed-ring and zwitterionic forms. We then use this knowledge to reprogram thioazole derivatives and render them into zwitterion-forming aza-DAEs. With these results, the predictable and rational design of aza-DAEs is enabled, which can now be radically changed in their photoresponses and tailored to specific desired properties and applications.

item.title: ACS Nano: Dissociating Spin and Charge Injections in Single-Molecule Junctions
item.description:
Hanjun Zhang, Yuling Zou, Fanxi Sun, Ignacio Rivas Mendoza, Sergio Moles Quintero, Mercedes Alonso, Xiaodong Liu, Yang Yang, et al.
Understanding the influence of organic radicals on single-molecule conductance is crucial for the development of nanoscale electronic devices. Radical ion systems reported to date typically exhibit both charge and spin effects acting simultaneously in the same manner. In this work, an attempt to separate these two effects is done by exploiting distinct spin injection and charge redistribution behaviors. We synthesized a series of nitronyl nitroxide (NNO) radical derivatives all sharing a common terphenyl conduction pathway. With the inclusion of one NNO unit, the positive charge is delocalized over the terphenyl, whereas the spin remains largely localized. Conversely, for two NNO units, charge injection is disfavored, whereas spin injection is favored, accompanied by a distinct charge redistribution involving the NNO units and the central ring. Using a scanning tunneling microscope break junction (STM-BJ) technique, we find the impacts of these two distinctive situations on the conductance of single-molecule junctions. Introduction of an NNO monoradical gives rise to a 2-fold increase in conductance due to the charge delocalization over the terphenyl. For the diradical, we observe a more substantial 4-fold increase in conductance (from 10–4.56G0 in the nonradical compound to 10–3.95G0), which can be attributed to electronic interaction between the two NNO units. A phenyl spacer is inserted between the NNO radical and the central phenyl ring in the terphenyl, which greatly suppresses the influence of the positive charge and spin effects on the conductance channel. Then, the radical-containing compounds with one and two NNO units present similar conductances emerging from rather different situations. Our findings elucidate the influence mechanisms of molecular structure and spin and charge localization/delocalization on single-molecule conductance, providing valuable insights for enhanced molecular electronic devices.

item.title: Nano Letters: Ultrafast Dissipative Localization of Electronic Energy in Au–Pt Superlattices
item.description:
C. Walz, M. Mattern, J.-E. Pudell, J. Jarecki, L. Mehner, F.-C. Weber, F. Baltrusch, S. P. Zeuschner, et al.
Controlling the spatial distribution of absorbed optical energy is central to nanoscale photothermal chemistry, plasmonics, and the ultrafast control of materials. Here, we show that a metallic Au–Pt superlattice concentrates electronic energy in Pt within a few hundred femtoseconds, regardless of the initial energy distribution between the two constituents. Ultrafast X-ray diffraction follows this energy redistribution through the amplitude of a coherent 570 GHz superlattice phonon driven by the stress imbalance at the Au–Pt interfaces. Despite the nearly homogeneous absorption at 400 nm, the observed lattice motion is identical to that produced by 800 nm excitation, which is absorbed predominantly in Pt. This dissipation-driven localization of energy arises from the large electronic heat capacity of Pt and rapid electronic transport through the superlattice, providing a route to femtosecond control of nanoscale energy distributions.

item.title: JACS: Stepwise Assembly of a Lavandulyl Moiety on Flavonoids Enabled by a 2″-Prenyltransferase
item.description:
Yang-oujie Bao, Meng Zhang, Zonglin Dai, Yi Chen, Min Ye
Lavandulylated flavonoids contain a characteristic branched C10 moiety, and the enzymatic basis underlying its biosynthesis remains poorly understood. Here, we elucidate the complete biosynthetic pathway of the lavandulylated flavonoid kurarinone from naringenin in the medicinal plant Sophora flavescens. The pathway involves four sequential steps, 8-prenylation, 2′-hydroxylation, 2″-prenylation, and 5-O-methylation, catalyzed by Sf8PT, SfF2′H, Sf2″PT, and Sf5OMT, respectively. Sf2′′PT represents the first characterized flavonoid 2′′-prenyltransferase (PT), catalyzing a second prenylation on the pre-existing prenyl side chain to complete the assembly of the branched lavandulyl moiety. The activity of Sf2″PT strictly depends on prior 2′-hydroxylation, establishing a defined order of enzymatic modifications that enables this noncanonical prenylation reaction. Ancestral sequence reconstruction and mutagenesis demonstrated that an inactive ancestral enzyme could be converted into functional 8PT or 2′′PT variants through one or seven amino acid substitutions, respectively. Collectively, this work establishes the enzymatic basis for stepwise lavandulyl moiety assembly and provides a framework for the enzymatic construction and engineering of branched prenylated natural products.

item.title: JACS: Hydrogen-Bond Network-Assisted Ethylene and Hydrogen Photosynthesis from Methane over Isolated Ir Active Sites under Ambient Conditions
item.description:
Fei Hong, Ruihui Gan, Baiyang Yu, Pengfei Du, Bing Yang, Jiawei Zhang, Jing Xu, Chengsi Pan, et al.
Direct conversion of methane to ethylene (DCM) is an attractive yet formidable challenge due to the difficult C–H activation and uncontrollable C–C coupling process. Herein, we report a hydrogen-bond network-assisted ethylene and H2 photosynthesis from methane over oxygen-vacancy-enriched TiO2-supported single Ir atoms (Ir1/TiO2–Ov) under ambient conditions. The Ir-induced lattice distortion drives spontaneous hydrolysis under humid conditions, generating a hydroxylated surface that endows coordinatively unsaturated Ir sites to activate the first methane molecule without light irradiation. Upon photoexcitation, surface hydroxyls are oxidized into dangling oxygen species (*O) on Ti sites, which promote the dehydrogenation of *CH3 to *CH2. In synergy with the Ir site, the adjacent *O species activate a second CH4 molecule and finally direct selective C–C coupling to form C2H4. Meanwhile, methane-derived protons migrate through the hydrogen-bond network via a Grotthuss mechanism to produce H2. The Ir1/TiO2–Ov catalyst achieves the production of ethylene (14.3 ± 0.7 μmol•gcat–1•h–1) and H2 (28.4 ± 1.2 μmol•gcat–1•h–1) for at least 210 h at 25 °C and atmospheric pressure under light irradiation. Our findings establish a hydrogen-bond network-assisted strategy for methane C–H activation and selective C–C and H–H coupling.

item.title: Nano Letters: Mapping Coupled Lattice Disorders at the Nanoscale via Infrared Near-Field Spectroscopy
item.description:
Ying Liao, Rao Fu, Mengfei Xue, Wentao Song, Jiarong Guo, Yang Wang, You Wu, Bo Wang, et al.
Coupled lattice disorders critically limit the performance of wide-bandgap semiconductor devices, yet their direct and quantitative characterization remains challenging. Here, we present a noninvasive spectroscopic framework to resolve multiple lattice disorder parameters based on nanoscale Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (nano-FTIR). By exploiting the sensitivity of infrared phonons to local lattice environments, this approach enables simultaneous mapping of compositional variation, point defects, phase segregation, and strain with ∼20-nm spatial resolution. In AlxGa1–xN, we directly visualize Al/Ga compositional variations within individual V-pits and detect SiGa point defects with a sensitivity approaching ∼30 dopant atoms. We further uncover a previously unresolved ∼350-nm-wide interfacial transition region at the AlN/AlxGa1–xN interface and quantify local tensile stress up to ∼6.3 GPa. By avoiding carrier diffusion and spatial averaging, this approach enables high-fidelity reconstruction of nanoscale lattice heterogeneity, establishing nano-FTIR as a general platform to guide epitaxial design and device optimization in semiconductor heterostructures.

item.title: JACS: Redox-Window-Guided Metal Node Editing of Copper Metal–Organic Frameworks for Recyclable Heterogeneous Cu(I) Catalysis
item.description:
Hye Mi Kim, Sun Ho Park, Jong Chan Chae, Dohyun Moon, Sunggi Lee, Nak Cheon Jeong
Cu(I) catalysts are central to many bond-forming reactions, but integrating Cu(I) sites into recyclable porous solids remains difficult because Cu(I) is easily oxidized, over-reduced, or leached. Here, we report redox-window-guided metal node editing as an oxidation-state-programming strategy that converts hydrolytically fragile Cu(II)3BTC2 into a hydrolytically stable mixed-valence Cu(I/II) MOF catalyst. Phenolic reductants are selected by matching their oxidation potentials to the Cu(II)–to–Cu(I) window of Cu(II)3BTC2, enabling proton-coupled, inner-sphere single-electron transfer at Cu paddlewheel nodes. Hydroquinone gives the most controlled material, [p-Ph(OH)2]-Cu3BTC2, containing 33.4% Cu(I), ship-in-a-bottle [Cu(MeCN)4]+ complexes, mesopores, and enhanced stability under humid, acidic, and basic conditions. As a heterogeneous catalyst for hydrative amide synthesis, [p-Ph(OH)2]-Cu3BTC2 affords 92% yield, negligible Cu leaching, five-cycle recyclability, and the highest turnover number among compared Cu(I) catalysts.

item.title: JACS: Synthetic Control of Quantum Phases in Organic Conductors: Molecular-Level Disorder Engineering and Pressure-Induced Superconductivity
item.description:
Soichiro Yasaka, Yukihiro Yoshida, Yusuke Nanba, Satoshi Iguchi, Yuka Ikemoto, Shiori Sugiura, Muhammad K. Nuryadin, Takahiko Sasaki, et al.
Structural randomness is a dominant factor governing electronic properties; however, the intrinsic effects of a disordered potential remain elusive due to the lack of a synthetic platform capable of introducing purely random potentials without carrier doping or altering the fundamental band structure. Here, we demonstrate the synthetic control of superconducting and insulating phases by exploiting the unique conformational flexibility of molecular conductors. Through precise thermodynamic control during crystal growth, we selectively synthesize the structurally ordered superconductor κ-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu[N(CN)2]Br (κ-Br; BEDT-TTF = bis(ethylenedithio)tetrathiafulvalene) and the structurally disordered insulating polymorph, κ″-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu[N(CN)2]Br (κ″-Br), possessing the exact same chemical composition. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations confirm the metastable nature of κ″-Br, showing a packing arrangement of BEDT-TTF molecules and an electronic band structure nearly identical to those of superconducting κ-Br, but featuring a disordered anion layer. Optical conductivity spectra reveal low-energy excitations without a distinct gap, indicating that the insulating behavior originates from disorder-induced carrier localization. Furthermore, κ″-Br undergoes a pressure-induced insulator–superconductor transition, in stark contrast to postsynthetic X-ray irradiation which induced irreversible structural damage. This work represents the first demonstration of synthetic control of an ordered superconductor and a disordered insulator driven solely by orientational disorder in organic conductors. Our study provides new avenues for manipulating strongly correlated electron systems and for investigating the intrinsic effects of randomness, free from carrier doping or structural perturbation of conducting layers.

item.title: JACS: Single-Atom Cerium Unlocks Efficient Hydrogen Spillover within Nonreducible Zeolites through a Proton–Electron Relay
item.description:
Xinlei Han, Shijun Gui, Kuizhi Chen, Wei Cao, Yihu Dai, Jiuxuan Zhang, Zhengyan Qu, Feng Zeng, et al.
Hydrogen spillover connects hydrogen activation with spatially separated catalytic functions, yet engineering efficient hydrogen transport through nonreducible zeolites remains an outstanding challenge owing to the absence of intrinsic pathways for coupled proton–electron transfer. Here, we show that isolated cerium atoms incorporated into Pt/USY transform the zeolite from a passive support into an active medium for solid-state hydrogen transport. In situ spectroscopy, isotopic tracing, and theoretical calculations reveal that atomically dispersed Ce species dynamically generate localized hydroxyl groups and oxygen vacancies that cooperatively establish a proton–electron relay, substantially lowering the kinetic barrier for hydrogen migration through zeolitic micropores. The resulting enhancement in hydrogen spillover extends hydrogen delivery to spatially remote Brønsted acid sites, suppresses coke formation, and significantly improves polyolefin hydrocracking stability. These findings establish hydrogen transport as a tunable design parameter in bifunctional zeolite catalysis and provide a general strategy for engineering hydrogen-transfer pathways in nonreducible porous materials.

item.title: JACS: Electron-Deficient β-Diketone Ligand Enabled Ni-Catalyzed Remote Dicarbofunctionalization of Alkenes
item.description:
Shuo Song, Dao-Ming Wang, Jin-Ping Wang, Yichen Wu, Peng Wang
A nickel-catalyzed remote migratory dicarbofunctionalization of alkenes was realized with high efficiency and excellent regioselectivity without the assistance of a directing group. The formation of a thermodynamically stable allyl-metal intermediate and the use of an electron-deficient β-diketone ligand are the keys to the success of these remote diarylation and arylalkenylation. This protocol features a broad substrate scope and excellent functional group compatibility, providing a series of remote diarylated and arylalkenylated hydrocarbons in high yields. Notably, the allyl group represents one of the most synthetically useful handles in synthetic chemistry, and the synthetic values of this process have been demonstrated by the formal synthesis of allocolchicinoids, and by the preparation of a RARγ selective retinoid agonist in a highly efficient and step-economical manner.

item.title: Nano Letters: Microscopic Understanding of Thermal Magnon Transport in Low-Damping Ferrimagnetic Thin Films
item.description:
Lerato Takana, Katya Mikhailova, Junwei Tong, Xiangcheng Liu, Kwangyul Hu, Juan A. Hofer, Guanxiong Qu, Clare C. Yu, et al.
Thermally generated magnons enable heat-driven spin transport in magnetic insulators, yet the relative importance of microscopic mechanisms governing their propagation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate thermal magnon transport in low-damping Li0.5Al1.0Fe1.5O4/Pt nanodevices by using a nonlocal spin Seebeck geometry that separates magnon transport from local thermoelectric effects. Thermal imaging establishes a detector region outside of the thermal healing length, enabling intrinsic nonlocal measurements. We find that thermal magnon transport is strongly suppressed by magnetic fields far above saturation and that thermal magnon transport decreases with increasing temperature despite an increasing magnon population. Brillouin light scattering reveals the key microscopic mechanism driving this effect: an increasing field reduces the group velocity of backward volume magnons, reducing the magnon spin diffusion length. Micromagnetic simulations reproduce this behavior only when temperature-dependent exchange stiffness is included. These results identify the magnon group velocity and exchange stiffness as parameters governing thermal magnon transport in ferrimagnetic thin films.

item.title: JACS: Revisiting the Biosynthetic Cyclization of Indole Sesquiterpene Alkaloids: Proposal of a Spiro -Indolenine Pathway and Synthesis of Prelecanindole
item.description:
Wataru Saito, Aya Takemoto, Yoko Kobayashi, Tadachika Miyasaka, Hajime Sato, Masanobu Uchiyama, Toshio Nishikawa
Indole sesquiterpene and indole diterpene alkaloids constitute a distinctive class of natural products characterized by complex polycyclic ring architectures and diverse potent biological activities. In indole sesquiterpenes, the characteristic indole-containing pentacyclic skeleton is biosynthesized from 3-farnesylindole through epoxidation followed by a sequential cationic cyclization. Although the cyclization enzyme has been identified, the details of its cyclization mechanism remain unclear. Here, we propose a new biosynthetic mechanism involving a spiro-indoleninium intermediate, which contrasts with the long-standing mechanism proposed in the 1970s that proceeds via a tertiary-to-secondary carbocation rearrangement. We demonstrated the feasibility of this new mechanism by means of density functional theory (DFT) calculations, which do not support the conventional mechanism and also by chemical emulation: the putative spiro-indolenine intermediate was synthesized from two fragments through stereoselective cyclopropanation as a key reaction and subsequently converted to prelecanindole, a common biosynthetic intermediate of indole sesquiterpene alkaloids, under mild acidic conditions.

item.title: JACS: Strengthening Metal–Oxygen Bonds via Ionicity–Covalency Asymmetric Connection: 4f Electronic Configuration Effect
item.description:
Jiamin Zhu, Zhuang Zhang, Yang Hu, Yaxiong Yao, Shanshan Wu, Wei Shen, Nan Zhang, Li An, et al.
Precise control over the characteristics of metal–oxygen (M–O) bonds by regulating the electron redistribution between the metal and oxygen under perturbation conditions is crucial for maintaining the structural stability of transition-metal oxides. However, its development has always been hindered by the strong coupling between orbital hybridization and charge localization. Herein, by leveraging the strong ionicity of the Ce–O bonds in CeO2, we constructed an ionicity–covalency asymmetric bonding network, in which the ionic Ce–O is atomically coupled with the covalent M–O (M = Ni/Co). The reduced Ce–O coordination in this special structure weakens the O 2p → Ce 4f charge transfer and further elevates the ionic character of Ce–O bonds, thereby activating the reversible 4f electronic configuration transition. Critically, this configuration undergoes reversible transformation under potential fluctuation, reshaping charge redistribution within the M–O bonding motifs and then suppressing irreversible M–O bond degradation. Harnessing this mechanism enables transition-metal oxides to express a robust framework for the whole structure under repeated redox cycling. Incorporating this resulting CeO2/NiCo2O4, a large-scale alkaline water electrolysis (AWE) stack delivers significantly stable operation for over 350 h at 6 A under a 12-h intermittent experimental protocol. This finding offers a fundamental insight into the dynamic charge distribution in M–O bonds under potential perturbation for universal structural protection.

item.title: Nano Letters: Atomic Termination Controls Interfacial Charge Transfer and Spin-Valley Coupling in MnBi4Te7/MoSe2 Heterostructures
item.description:
Siyu Zhang, Xian Zhang, Junying Chen, Shikun Hou, Yixuan Chen, Jun He, Zongwen Liu, Yanping Liu
Van der Waals magnetic heterostructures enable interfacial control of excitonic and valley responses, but how atomic termination governs these interactions remains unclear. Here we investigate hBN-encapsulated MnBi4Te7/MoSe2 heterostructures through spatially resolved optical spectroscopy, magneto-photoluminescence, and first-principles calculations. The heterostructures exhibit pronounced photoluminescence quenching, enhanced charged-exciton emission, and spatially distinct red-shifted and blue-shifted excitonic regimes. Comparisons with ideal Bi2Te3- and MnBi2Te4-terminated interface models suggest competing contributions from dielectric screening, interfacial charge separation, and hybridization with metallic states. Helicity-resolved Raman measurements reveal spatially varying polarization responses, while magneto-photoluminescence uncovers hysteretic valley polarization with a coercive field of approximately 0.1 T. These findings highlight the sensitivity of excitonic and valley responses to local interfacial electronic structure, suggesting atomic termination as a potential parameter for engineering magnetic semiconductor heterostructures, while motivating direct structural identification of buried interfaces.

item.title: JACS: A Bioinspired Thiolate-Bridged Diiron System for Functionally Replicating Hydrazine Dehydrogenase and Its Efficient Electrocatalytic Hydrazine Oxidation
item.description:
Chunyan Wang, Zihe Song, Ronghuan Du, Hui Jiang, Dawei Yang, Jingping Qu
Hydrazine dehydrogenase (HDH) catalyzes the oxidation of hydrazine (N2H4) to dinitrogen (N2) as the final step of anaerobic ammonium oxidation, an essential process in closing the nitrogen cycle. Despite extensive biochemical studies, the detailed mechanism of HDH at a molecular level remains elusive. An increasing number of studies indicate that the hydrazine oxidation reaction (HzOR) is also central to direct hydrazine fuel cells. However, known electrocatalysts for HzOR are predominantly heterogeneous systems, while molecular electrocatalysts are still scarce, especially those inspired by biological HDH. This scarcity not only limits mechanistic understanding but also hinders the development of efficient and tunable catalysts. To tackle these challenging issues, we sought inspiration from the biological HDH system, wherein multiple iron-containing heme subunits cooperatively promote efficient HzOR with the assistance of surrounding sulfur-bearing cysteine residues. Integrating these key features, we selected the thiolate-bridged diiron complex [Cp*Fe(μ-SEt)(MeCN)]2[PF6]2 (1, Cp* = η5-C5Me5) for functionally replicating HDH. Treatment of 1 with N2H4 induces disproportionation to afford the active diazene (N2H2) species, which can be captured by the diiron cooperative platform to yield [Cp*Fe(μ-SEt)2(cis-μ-η1:η1-HN=NH)FeCp*][PF6] (2). In the presence of appropriate electron and proton acceptors, complex 2 undergoes a two-electron oxidation, leading to N2 release and the regeneration of 1. Remarkably, both complexes 1 and 2 serve as efficient molecular electrocatalysts for HzOR. This diiron molecular system not only achieves the functional replication of HDH involving a key N2H2 intermediate but also establishes a bioinspired design strategy for developing multimetal cooperative electrocatalysts toward efficient HzOR.

item.title: JACS: Electrochemical Allylic Carboxylation of Unactivated Alkenes with CO2
item.description:
Wei Zhang, Chuan-Kun Ran, Li Li, Long-Fei Dai, Guo-Quan Sun, Jun-Ping Yue, Li-Li Liao, Lei Song, et al.
As both alkenes and CO2 are abundant and easily available feedstocks, carboxylation of alkenes with CO2 represents an attractive and sustainable strategy to synthesize value-added carboxylic acids. Despite substantial advances in carboxylation of π-bonds in alkenes, the carboxylation of C–H bonds in alkenes, which preserves the C═C bond in the synthesis of valuable unsaturated carboxylic acids, remains a longstanding challenge, particularly for unactivated alkenes owing to their intrinsically low reactivity. Herein, we report the first electrochemical allylic carboxylation of unactivated alkenes with CO2, providing a direct and selective approach to hard-to-obtain β,γ-unsaturated carboxylic acids. Moreover, this reaction exhibits a broad substrate scope, good functional group tolerance, and applicability to late-stage diversification. Mechanistic studies indicate that the electrogenerated CO2 radical anion acts both as the carboxylation reagent and the hydrogen-atom abstraction species for the subsequent desaturation process, further uncovering the synthetic utility potential of the CO2 radical anion.

item.title: JACS: Immobilizing Ionomers by Strong Hydrogen Bonds for Highly Stable Industrial Water Electrolysis at 3.0 A/cm2
item.description:
Han Liu, Heng Duan, Siyuan Han, Linrui Wen, Linyuan Chen, Meiquan Huang, Xueyi Wang, Tian Hu, et al.
Raising the operating current density can effectively reduce the high cost of proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs), but this approach is limited by rapid electrode degradation. Our previous research identified a critical degradation mechanism in which ionomer migration blocks mass-transport channels in the anode catalyst layer (ACL). Here, we find that each sulfonate group of the ionomer forms only about half a hydrogen bond on the IrO2 surface, indicating a weak catalyst–ionomer interaction. Rather than modifying the IrO2 surface, we propose to introduce additives that provide additional adsorption sites forming stronger hydrogen bonds (SHB) with the sulfonate groups. The resulting SHB-ACL maintains a stable ionomer distribution and pore network even after aging, and exhibits a roughly four fold lower degradation rate over 2500 h at 3.0 A/cm2. Furthermore, the electrode can be readily scaled up to 600 cm2. The improvement stability is at least in part attributable to enhanced interface interaction, although preserved porosity, water/gas transport, and interparticle contacts may also contribute. These findings offer a scalable route toward durable industrial PEMWE devices.

item.title: ACS Nano: Ratiometric Multispectral Upconversion-Photoacoustic Nanoprobes for Noninvasive Imaging of Hepatic and Urinary Copper Dynamics in Wilson’s Disease
item.description:
Yi Zhou, Hui Zhang, Yifan Li, Jinshuang Hu, Yuanjun Li, Yiliang Yin, Yuhan Shen, Jingyun Li, et al.
Wilson’s disease (WD) is an inherited disorder of copper metabolism, and the lack of a noninvasive, real-time monitoring method for copper accumulation presents a significant clinical challenge. Herein, we report a galactose-targeted, dual-modal ratiometric nanoprobe, termed Cu-MB, which integrates multispectral upconversion luminescence (mUCL) and multispectral photoacoustic tomography (mPAT) for the sensitive, specific, and dynamic visualization of hepatic copper in deep tissues. The nanoprobe features a Cu2+-responsive NIR-II chromophore (Cu-RB) and an internal reference dye coloaded onto upconversion nanoparticles, enabling self-calibrated quantification via the ratiometric signals of PA930/PA680 and UCL660/UCL800. This design effectively corrects for environmental interference and offers superior tissue penetration. In WD mouse models, Cu-MB enables real-time, longitudinal monitoring of hepatic copper deposition and accurately quantifies urinary copper excretion, showing excellent correlation with the clinical gold standard (ICP-MS). Furthermore, it allows for the visual assessment of the efficacy of copper chelation therapies (e.g., EDTA and D-pen). Notably, in a blinded clinical validation using human urine samples, the mPAT signal from Cu-MB achieved high diagnostic accuracy in this preliminary cohort, showing a clear separation trend between WD patients and healthy controls. This work presents a robust nanoprobe platform for noninvasive imaging of copper dynamics, enabling the diagnosis, dynamic monitoring, and therapeutic evaluation of Wilson’s disease.

item.title: JACS: Ligand-Controlled Chemodivergent β-Methylene C(sp3)–H Heteroarylation of Aliphatic Acids
item.description:
Liang Hu, Yilin Lu, Xiang-Lei Han, Jie-Lun Yan, Tao Sheng, T. G. Murali Dhar, Shuang Liu, Renyu Guo, et al.
Achieving ligand-controlled chemodivergence in C–H activation is still difficult because several competing reaction pathways are available when multiple C–H bonds are present. We describe a Pd(II)-catalyzed, chemodivergent β-methylene C(sp3)–H heteroarylation of free aliphatic acids in which two distinct classes of bidentate pyridone ligands each deliver a different product. These two ligands also overcome a long-standing inhibitory effect of heteroaryl iodides, demonstrating the potential of this protocol to serve as a general C(sp3)–C(sp2) coupling method using readily available aliphatic acids as the alkylating partner. Mechanistic experiments and DFT analyses reveal that π–π stacking between the quinoline motif and the heteroaryl ring lowers the barrier for rotation of the carbon–palladium bond, favoring protodepalladation to the reductive Heck product, whereas the oxime ether ligand lacks this interaction and steers the key intermediate toward β-H elimination to give the oxidative Heck product.

item.title: JACS: Cation Pinning toward High-Concentration Formic Acid Fuel Cells
item.description:
Kai Wei, Xian Wang, Mingzi Sun, Huan Liu, Lin Lin, Li Yi, Yunxiang Wang, Siming Gao, et al.
Despite the high theoretical energy density of concentrated formic acid, direct formic acid fuel cells (DFAFCs) incorporating conventional nanoparticle or emerging single-atom anodes exhibit a precipitous power loss as fuel concentration scales. While CO poisoning is traditionally blamed, we show that this limitation is governed by interfacial acid–base kinetics. By implementing a cation-pinning strategy via rare-earth oxide-modified Rh single-atom sites, we stabilize OH– from water dissociation through interfacial ionic anchoring to trigger localized pH inversion. This modulation leads to the preferential enrichment of interfacial formate, identified here as the primary reactive species. Consequently, Dy2O3–Rh/NC delivers a mass activity 641-fold higher than that of nanoparticle benchmarks. The resulting anode achieves an exceptional peak power density of 375 mW cm–2, surpassing commercial Pd/C across all concentrations. This work establishes precision ionic management as a versatile approach to breaking performance limits in multiphase catalysis.

item.title: JACS: In Situ High-Pressure NMR Reveals Pressure-Defect Generation in Aluminum Acetylacetonate toward Integrated Optical Response
item.description:
Kaixiang Jin, Binhao Yang, Shanyu Zheng, Tiantong Wang, Jiaxin Wang, Peixi Zhou, Yuanqing Li, Kewei Zhang, et al.
Stimuli-responsive luminescent materials featuring real-time pressure-response with persistent memory effects hold considerable promise for advanced photonic computing. However, most pressure-memory behavior depends on triggered irreversible phase transitions, which hinders the integration of reversible optical sensing. Synergistic pressure treatment and defect generation serve as an effective approach that ensures the phase-transition-free structure while affording excellent photoluminescence (PL) performance. In this work, we employ pressure-defect generation strategy in aluminum acetylacetonate that effectively integrates short-term pressure response with long-term history memory. Notably, the PL wavelength acts as a digital readout across 476–486 nm, alongside an intensity-based analog signal below 4 GPa. Upon crossing this threshold, the response further embeds memory states dependent on pressure history. In situ high-pressure nuclear magnetic resonance (HP-NMR) measurements reveal, from both static and dynamic perspectives, the progressive deepening of pressure-induced local responses within the molecular framework, from ligand-associated modulation to Al–O coordination perturbation. This establishes a two-regime pressure-defect generation pathway: reversible structural distortion induces electronic-state defects, whereas partially trapped severe distortion may generate radical defects. Our work not only highlights the unique capability of local dynamic probing for the design of pressure-responsive materials, but also broadens the horizons of single-material multifunctional information-processing systems.

item.title: JACS: Bioinspired Ångström-Scale Coupling of Reductive Centers in Covalent Organic Frameworks Drives Efficient Photocatalytic Oxygen Reduction
item.description:
Penghan Ding, Yongqi Pan, Kai Min, Hongli Zhou, Yujun Wang, Qiang Chen
The photocatalytic oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) is crucial for solar-to-chemical energy conversion but faces challenges from weak oxygen adsorption and slow kinetics. Inspired by the spatially cooperative multimetal centers in natural enzymes, we develop a strategy of Å-scale spatial coupling of reductive centers in covalent organic frameworks (COFs). Ortho-amino-functionalized COFs were constructed with catalytic pockets that position multiple acceptors within subnanometer proximity, creating coupled reductive centers for cooperative O2 adsorption and multielectron relay. The optimal framework, with a model-derived separation of approximately 3.3 Å between reductive centers, achieves a hydrogen peroxide production rate of 4.10 mmol g–1 h–1 in pure water under visible light without sacrificial agents, along with a high apparent quantum yield of 19.2% at 450 nm. Practical viability is confirmed through operation in diverse water sources and continuous-flow systems. Moreover, the enhanced ORR activity accelerates oxidative coupling of benzylamine derivatives, showing over 80% conversion for 12 analogues. Experimental and theoretical analyses indicate that the confined neighboring sites enhance O2 adsorption and activation, stabilize •OOH intermediates, and promote the two-electron reduction pathway. This work establishes convergent multicenter coupling as a foundational design principle, unlocking new avenues for the rational creation of high-performance photocatalysts in sustainable chemistry.

item.title: JACS: A Cu-Modified Layered Thiostannate for Selective Pb Capture from Strongly Acidic Media
item.description:
Dimitrios A. Evangelou, Patricia E. Meza, Jinlei Cui, Xiangyu Ma, Elias M. Kallon, Anastasia D. Pournara, Christos D. Malliakas, Alexios P. Douvalis, et al.
Layered metal sulfide ion exchangers are powerful platforms for soft-metal capture, but their application in strongly acidic environments requires framework stability while preserving accessible ion-exchange pathways. Here, we introduce a new series of Cu-modified SnS2-derived layered chalcogenides, AMS-8 (A = Na, K, Rb, Cs), featuring labile interlayer alkali metal ions. NMS-8 (Na1.13Cu1.32Sn3.34S8·xH2O) demonstrates that Cu+ can be incorporated into the SnS2-derived AMS layered motif without disrupting the fundamental architecture. Upon acid exposure, NMS-8 undergoes Na+/H+ exchange and interlayer contraction, showing low Sn leaching in 6 M H2SO4 but substantial Sn dissolution in 6 M HCl after prolonged exposure, despite persistent powder X-ray diffraction reflections of the layered phase. NMS-8 can rapidly capture Pb2+ from water, achieving near-complete removal within 20 s under dilute conditions, a Sips-fitted capacity of 178.2 ± 12.4 mg g–1 (regression standard error), and high selectivity against common competing cations. Structural characterization supports preservation of the lamellar network and a proposed structural model featuring Cu+ displaced off-center within a distorted octahedral framework environment. In an acid mine drainage simulant, NMS-8 selectively removes Pb, Cd, and Cu under acidic multicomponent conditions while retaining its layered structure. Local structural characterization of NMS-8@Pb reveals a spatially heterogeneous Pb distribution within individual crystallites that is not appropriately described by a simple homogeneous interlayer exchange model and is consistent with local structural reorganization during Pb2+ uptake. These results highlight Cu-modified layered thiostannates as promising platforms for rapid, selective soft-metal capture, with substantial resistance to concentrated sulfuric acid and Pb retention dependent on the leaching medium.

item.title: JACS: Negative-Charge-Transfer Ligand Holes Enhance Ferromagnetism and Topological Transport in van der Waals Magnets
item.description:
Yuxuan Zhou, Ke Yang, Feng-Ren Fan, Yaozhenghang Ma, Hua Wu
Many prototypical 3d van der Waals (vdW) magnets contain heavy ligands with closed p shells, whose strong spin–orbit coupling (SOC) influences the magnetism only indirectly through p–d hybridization. Here we show that negative charge transfer (NCT) creates spin-polarized, SOC-active holes in the ligand p states bordering the vdW gap, coupling magnetic exchange and topological transport within the same states. First-principles calculations identify the synthesized MnSiTe3 as an NCT d5L ferromagnet comprising high-spin Mn2+ and one formal Te 5p ligand hole per f.u. The Te-derived holes strengthen both intralayer and, in particular, interlayer ferromagnetic exchange, favoring ferromagnetic over antiferromagnetic interlayer order by a surprisingly large 84.1 meV/f.u. SOC within the partially occupied Te 5p manifold produces an easy-plane magnetocrystalline anisotropy of 3.6 meV/f.u. The resulting simulated Curie temperature reaches 464 K. The SOC-active Te 5p holes further generate multiple Weyl points, yielding a calculated intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity of 760 Ω–1 cm–1 that remains large over a broad energy window around the Fermi level. All those results stand in sharp contrast to ligand-shell-closed vdW magnets. This NCT ligand-hole picture and the resulting magnetic and transport responses also extend to the synthesized MnGeTe3 and the predicted iodides Cr0.5Mn0.5I3 and MnI3. These results establish NCT as a chemical strategy that makes the vdW interface magnetically and topologically active. Substituting later 3d metals or heavier p ligands into existing vdW magnets drives them toward the NCT regime, providing a design principle for the discovery of new NCT candidates.

item.title: Nano Letters: One-Dimensional Hybrid Metal Halides as Tunable Chiral THz Emitters
item.description:
Joanna M. Urban, Oliver Gueckstock, Michael S. Spencer, Genaro Bierhance, Olga Minakova, Maximilian Frenzel, Abdelaziz Jouaiti, Jean-Luc Bruneel, et al.
Recent progress in chirality-related phenomena in condensed matter physics drives the demand for tailored terahertz (THz) fields to investigate and manipulate helicity-dependent low-energy excitations in solids and molecules. Controlling polarization and helicity of THz pulses is essential for probing and directing angular momentum transfer and chiral phononics. However, manipulating the THz helicity remains challenging, requiring inherently chiral, tunable THz emitters. Here, we demonstrate THz emission from one-dimensional lead bromide compounds with chiral organic cations under femtosecond near-infrared excitation, arising from chirality transfer-induced symmetry breaking. Nonresonant optical rectification yields a broadband contribution and a long-lived narrowband oscillation at 4.7 THz, dominated by an optical phonon. The emitted THz field’s polarization and spectrum can be tuned by adjusting the generation beam’s polarization relative to the crystalline axes, enabling spectral and polarization tuning. Our findings establish chiral low-dimensional hybrid organic–inorganic metal-halide perovskites as a vast library of tunable THz emitters.

item.title: ACS Nano: A Pd Single-Atom/Nanocluster Nanozyme Achieves High Dual Peroxidase- and Catalase-like Activities via Interlayer-Confined Oxygen-Species Spillover
item.description:
Jie Yang, Xixi Zhang, Qiang Zhang, Shichao Zhao, Yong Qin, Ruiping Zhang
Nanozymes that reproduce the multienzyme antioxidant machinery of living tissue remain difficult to engineer because the atomic sites that most strongly activate H2O2 also bind the reaction intermediates too tightly to release them─a trade-off, rooted in the Sabatier principle, that often caps the activity of single-atom catalysts. Here, we report an atomically dispersed palladium nanozyme, Pd1+NPs/G, in which isolated Pd single atoms and ultrasmall Pd nanoclusters coexist on graphene oxide (GO) and propose, based on density functional theory (DFT) calculations and isotope labeling, that this architecture relieves this trade-off through an interlayer-confined hydroxyl (*OH) spillover mechanism. Prepared by atomic layer deposition, Pd1+NPs/G exhibits the highest mass-normalized peroxidase (POD)-like and catalase (CAT)-like activities among its single-atom (Pd1/G) and nanoparticle (PdNPs/G) counterparts, with 18- and 8-fold higher specific activities than Pd1/G. DFT calculations indicate that the Pd single atom acts as a strong-binding electron-donor site and the Pd cluster as a moderate-binding acceptor site; an *OH intermediate is proposed to migrate across the ∼7–10 Å GO interlayer gap between them with a barrier of only 0.34 eV, enabling O–O coupling on the cluster, consistent with the observed 16O18O isotope scrambling. This spatial decoupling of the activation and desorption steps drives simultaneously efficient •OH generation and O2 evolution. The dual activity translates into H2O2-enhanced killing of Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, macrophage M1 → M2 repolarization, enhanced angiogenesis, and accelerated closure of S. aureus-infected wounds in vivo without detectable systemic toxicity. This work establishes support-geometry-directed oxygen-species spillover as a design principle for high-activity synergistic nanozymes.

item.title: JACS: Asymmetric Partial Hydrogenation of Quinazolines: Overcoming Catalyst Poisoning by a Robust yet Active Solo-Coordination-Vacant Ir(III) Pincer Catalyst
item.description:
De-Hai Liu, Cheng-Yu Gu, Gang Chen, Yun-Peng Chu, Yuan-Liang Zou, Chuanyong Wang, Constantin G. Daniliuc, Jiajia Ma
Catalytic asymmetric partial hydrogenation of quinazolines to afford enantioenriched 3,4-dihydroquinazolines, a privileged scaffold in medicinal chemistry, is a long-standing challenge likely due to product-induced catalyst deactivation. Here, we report a robust yet highly reactive solo-coordination-vacant Ir(III) pincer catalyst being capable of overcoming this poisoning challenge. This catalyst enables the asymmetric partial hydrogenation of a broad range of quinazolines, affording 3,4-dihydroquinazolines in high yields (up to 98%) and excellent enantioselectivities (up to 99% ee). In a dedicated catalyst-loading study, the loading could be reduced to 0.001 mol % (10 ppm, TON = 38,000). Mechanistic investigations, including NMR spectroscopic detection of a key Ir–H intermediate and base-dependence studies, support a catalytic cycle proceeding through a well-defined Ir(III)-hydride species and suggest that an alkali-metal-assisted pathway is unlikely to be dominant.

item.title: JACS: Local Molecular Motions Encode Time-Resolved Infrared Spectra of Proteins
item.description:
Emanuel Dorbath, Peter Hamm, Gerhard Stock
Time-resolved infrared spectroscopy probes protein dynamics over time scales spanning more than 10 orders of magnitude, yet the molecular motions underlying the observed kinetic signatures have remained elusive. Here we combine transient infrared spectroscopy with nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations to establish a direct connection between experimental relaxation times and local structural motions. Studying single-domain allosteric proteins, we find that inter-residue contact distances provide the structural representation that most faithfully reproduces the experimental dynamics. Correlation analysis identifies localized networks of coordinated contacts that mediate long-range coupling between secondary-structure elements. The characteristic time scales of these contact networks quantitatively match the experimentally observed relaxation processes, enabling each kinetic step to be assigned to a specific molecular motion. Applied to allosteric signal propagation in PDZ3 and photoinduced perturbation of the binding pocket of PDZ2 or a ligand binding to PDZ2, this framework provides an atomistic picture of hierarchical protein relaxation and establishes a general framework for connecting transient infrared spectroscopy with the molecular mechanisms of protein dynamics.

item.title: Nano Letters: Titanyl Phosphate: A Long-Life Anode Material for Mg-Ion Storage in Aqueous Batteries
item.description:
Chuanzheng Zhu, Qi Jiang, Ruihang Wen, Shihao Li, Mengdan Tian, Kun Luo
Aqueous magnesium-ion batteries (AMIBs) are considered as a promising system for energy storage. However, passivation, hydrogen evolution, and sluggish kinetics of metallic Mg anodes limit AMIB development, making alternative intercalation anodes a viable route. In this work, we report a novel titanium phosphate-based intercalation anode, Π-type Ti2O(PO4)2 (Π-TOP), which is modified through single transition metal element doping with Cr to form Π-Cr0.17Ti1.83O(PO4)2 (Π-CrTOP). The Π-CrTOP anode exhibits a reversible capacity of 137.2 mAh g–1 and a capacity retention of 98.5% after 2,200 cycles. Furthermore, an aqueous Mg-ion full cell using a VFePBA cathode and a Π-CrTOP anode delivers a reversible capacity of 125.4 mAh g–1 within 0.1–1.8 V and maintains stability for 6,000 cycles at room temperature. More importantly, our full cells can cycle 1,000 times at a low working temperature of −30 °C. This work provides a new perspective for the development of practically applicable AMIBs.

item.title: JACS: Dynamic Li+/Na+-Exchanging Interphase Stabilizes High-Voltage Ni-Rich Cathodes for 557 Wh kg–1 Lithium Batteries
item.description:
Wenjie Niu, Ning Zhao, Zizhuo Liang, Pengfei Yu, Zhangquan Peng, Guangmin Zhou, Xiangxin Guo
High-voltage operation of Ni-rich layered cathodes LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 (NCM811) accelerates electrolyte decomposition at the surface and destabilizes the bulk lattice with oxygen loss. Conventional strategies for regulating the cathode–electrolyte interphase (CEI) commonly suppress persistent parasitic reactions at Ni-rich cathode surfaces, but increase interfacial polarization and offer limited protection against structural degradation in the bulk. Here, a dynamic interphase is constructed by coating NCM811 with a Na+-based solid-electrolyte Na3Zr2Si2PO12 (NZSP). During cycling, Li+/Na+ exchange transforms the NZSP layer into a fast Li+ conducting interphase LixNa3–xZr2Si2PO12 (L-NZSP), while the Na+ ions are incorporated into the NCM811 lattice. The L-NZSP suppresses parasitic reactions at high charging voltages. Meanwhile, the incorporated Na+ ions provide pillar-like support for the layered framework, stabilizing the oxygen lattice and mitigating chemo-mechanical degradation. Consequently, the modified cathode retains 80% capacity after 511 cycles at 4.7 V and enables a 4 Ah pouch cell to deliver 557 Wh kg–1 with 80.5% retention over 118 cycles. This work demonstrates Li+/Na+-exchanging interphase as an effective strategy to couple interfacial protection with bulk lattice reinforcement for high-voltage Ni-rich cathodes in high-energy lithium batteries.

item.title: JACS: A Bowl-Shaped B,N-Tetraquinane Organic Super-Reductant
item.description:
Gan Xu, Zihan Li, Xinglong Zhang, Zhenpin Lu
Developing a stable molecular reductant with exceptionally strong reducing power remains highly challenging. In this work, we synthesized and characterized a bowl-shaped B–N tetraquinane in a single high-yield step. Cyclic voltammetry reveals a reduction potential of −3.2 V vs Fc/Fc+, a new record among organic reductants. This super-reductant enables [3 + 2] cycloadditions with ketones and imines, dearomatization of phthalazine, cleavage of strong C–Si bonds, direct reduction–borylation of fluorobenzene, deoxygenative coupling of nitrosobenzene, and ring-opening C–C coupling of aromatics into polyenes. Computational studies support its synthetic pathway, ring strain, high reactivity, and remarkably negative reduction potential. These findings demonstrate how three-dimensional topological strain can transform a boron-based dianion into a powerful reagent for reductive reactions and demanding bond activations.

item.title: JACS: Subambient Synthesis of Freestanding Monolayer Cubic ZrO2 Crystals with High Dielectric Permittivity
item.description:
Haofeng Sun, Xinyu Sun, Yufeng Min, Yuhang Guo, Haofeng Zhang, Yelun Cong, Xiaolin Tai, Minghao Wang, et al.
Two-dimensional (2D) polymorphic materials offer access to unconventional crystal structures that trigger exotic properties and functionalities beyond equilibrium phases. However, extending this opportunity to metal oxides remains highly challenging because both thickness reduction and phase transformation involve large energy barriers in such strongly bonded ionic structures. Here we report an atomic-freezing conversion strategy that kinetically stabilizes freestanding 2D metastable oxide crystals under subambient conditions. Single-crystalline cubic ZrO2 of monolayer thickness is produced and stabilized below room temperature, although this phase is typically stable only at temperatures above 2000 °C in bulk. Structural analysis reveals that the layered ZrNCl precursor contains a Zr atomic framework that matches the (111) planes of cubic ZrO2. During conversion, suppressed atomic motion under low temperatures and 2D confinement preserves the nonequilibrium cubic structure. The resulting 2D cubic ZrO2 exhibits a high dielectric permittivity of ∼23.5 and enables MoS2 field-effect transistors with an on/off ratio of ∼108 and a subthreshold slope as low as 63.5 mV dec–1. This approach also applies to cubic HfO2 and tetragonal Bi2O3, providing a general kinetic route to bypass thermodynamic phase constraints and expanding access to metastable oxides in the 2D limit.
